summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but Lima operates under a national framework that has legislated against trans people's use of public space. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, promulgated as the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, subject to listed exceptions. The provision followed the February 2025 approval, unanimously, by the congressional Women and Family Commission of the Muñante initiative presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia.

The same legislative package bars inclusive restroom signage of the kind Lima's international airport, Jorge Chávez, had installed, signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity", and prohibits wording such as "women in their diversity". LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, quoted on the measure, described how enforcement would reduce to security staff checking a national identity document (DNI) and deciding on their own judgement whether a woman entering a facility is trans.

IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, analysed the rule on 15 April 2025 as direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and observed that trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination. The institute also documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and found that the provision implicitly casts trans and non-binary people as harassment risks.

The restriction reaches private life as well. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people was removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023; more than half of the dead were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. The year 2023 saw the most homicides (19), and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One killing in Lima is on the record in detail: on 12 February 2023 the 31-year-old transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. Human-rights monitors flag state inaction in such cases: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's departure from regional practice is measurable: after the 2017 repeal it stands with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, while most of the continent retains such provisions.

The Inter-American human-rights machinery has been the effective route to accountability. The Azul Rojas Marín case travelled from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to the Inter-American Court, which issued the region's first torture-by-discrimination ruling, and Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 binds Peru to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy.

Recorded hate crimes are rising nationally, with trans women the most affected group, and the figures themselves are contested as a floor rather than a count. Monitors attribute the gap to the absence of any official system recording victims' sexual orientation, which allows hate crimes to go unsanctioned.

Public debate carries a documented hostility that a visitor may encounter directly. Congress floor speeches comparing trans people in dehumanising terms, and a television presenter directing a legislator to a men's restroom, indicate the register of mainstream commentary around the facilities rule.

Child-protection framing is being used to widen the censorship surface: vague articles in the April 2025 law reach media and advertising content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rose from three to four years, which Human Rights Watch reads as repression and scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
The facilities rule binds residents as a matter of daily compliance: restroom entry is set by biological sex as recorded at birth, and the ban on inclusive signage removes "women in their diversity" and similar wording from public-facing use. Enforcement rests largely on private security checking a DNI, so the practical exposure falls on anyone whose presentation prompts a check.

Trans residents have no hate-crime protection under the Penal Code following the 2017 repeal, and official statistics on homophobic and transphobic killings are collected only through civil-society observatories; the TLGBI Rights Observatory recorded 54 murders and 170 rights-violation reports between 2020 and 2023, with 26 of the 54 killings unsolved.

Healthcare access improved on one front in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance. A July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court, obtained after an activist legal challenge, struck down an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional, offering a domestic judicial route that the national legislature has not taken.

Discrimination complaints have limited reach: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's claim against a gym enforcing the restroom policy, indicating that administrative redress over the facilities rule should not be assumed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether article 5 of the April 2025 law has been challenged before the constitutional court, and what any such challenge's status is, is not sourced in this inventory.

Unresolved: no enforcement data is available on how often the DNI-check practice has been applied at Lima facilities, or how many complaints have followed; the account of security-staff enforcement comes from activist testimony rather than official records.

Unresolved: whether the signage prohibition extends to privately owned premises, or applies only to state-run and regulated facilities, is not stated in the sources reviewed.

Unresolved: the appeal status of the dismissed gym complaint, and whether the consumer-protection body's decision has been reviewed by a court, is not sourced.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no figure for the number of Lima residents or visitors affected by the facilities rule, and no census-based count of trans residents in the city.
